scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a policy response that backs informing students about pay while arguing against pushing them toward money; two developed examples weighing consequences, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Many students hope their studies will one day lead to a comfortable income.
One proposed policy is that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields that lead to lucrative careers.
I agree that schools should inform students about earnings, but I believe actively pushing them toward money would do harm.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why informing about earnings helps

sentences.text: First, helping students understand which fields pay well is genuinely useful.
Money affects nearly every part of life, from housing to health to raising a family.
For example, a student warned that a field pays very little can plan her finances more wisely.
This shows that honest information about pay can protect students from later regret.
Schools that share clear facts about careers help students make realistic and informed choices.
Knowing the likely rewards of a field can also reduce anxiety about the future.
To this extent, informing students about earnings is a sensible policy.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why pushing toward money harms

sentences.text: Second, however, actively pushing students toward lucrative careers could do real damage.
Students steered into high-paying fields they dislike may end up miserable and unsuccessful.
Consider a gifted teacher or artist pressured into finance who performs poorly and feels trapped.
Such outcomes show that chasing money alone can waste both talent and happiness.
Society also needs nurses, teachers, and artists, not only the highest-paid professionals.
Pushing everyone toward money could leave vital but modest careers badly understaffed.
Guidance, then, should inform students about pay without pressuring them to chase it.
In conclusion, schools are right to tell students honestly which careers pay well.
But actively pushing them toward money would ignore talent, interest, and the needs of society.
The wiser policy informs students about earnings while leaving the choice of career to them.
